questions.q: Which command scaffolds a brand-new Salesforce DX project with the standard folder layout already in place?
options: sf org create scratch
sf project generate --name my-project
sf project deploy start
sf project retrieve start
questions.explain: sf project generate --name my-project creates a new directory with the full standard Salesforce DX project structure already scaffolded, ready for metadata to be added.

questions.q: In the standard project layout, where does a project's actual Apex class and custom object metadata typically live?
options: Directly in the project root
Inside config/project-scratch-def.json
Under force-app/main/default/, in subfolders like classes/ and objects/
Inside .forceignore
questions.explain: force-app/main/default/ is the conventional default package directory, with per-metadata-type subfolders such as classes/ for Apex and objects/ for custom objects and fields.

questions.q: What is the role of sfdx-project.json in a Salesforce DX project?
options: It stores scratch org login credentials
It's the root configuration file defining the project's package directories, namespace, and API version
It's an alternate name for the .forceignore file
It stores a project's Git commit history
questions.explain: sfdx-project.json is the root configuration for the whole project — where its package directories are, which namespace it's tied to (if any), and its target API version — covered in full in Lesson 8.

options: It deletes files from the local project permanently
It tells the CLI which local files to exclude from deploy and retrieve operations, using .gitignore-style patterns
It defines which Apex tests run during deployment
It lists every org the CLI has authenticated to
questions.explain: .forceignore excludes specified files or folders from CLI deploy/retrieve operations, following the same pattern syntax as .gitignore.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say deviating from the standard project folder structure causes problems, even though nothing breaks outright?
options: Salesforce actively blocks nonstandard folder names at the API level

Every piece of Salesforce DX tooling (the CLI, VS Code extensions, CI pipelines) assumes the standard layout, so deviating means telling every tool explicitly where things are instead of it just working
Nonstandard structures are illegal under Salesforce's terms of service
It causes scratch orgs to expire immediately
questions.explain: The CLI and other tooling assume the conventional layout to find things automatically (e.g. sfdx-project.json's package directories); deviating doesn't technically break deploys, but it removes the "just works" convenience every tool is built around.
